analysis.one_liner: Bans seismic airgun blasting for oil and gas exploration along the Atlantic coast.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and its Energy subcommittee in 2016 and died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have blocked companies from using seismic airgun blasts — loud underwater sound surveys used to find oil and gas deposits under the ocean floor — across the North Atlantic, Mid-Atlantic, South Atlantic, and Straits of Florida planning areas off the US coast. The blasts are a first step toward offshore drilling, and scientists and coastal communities worry they harm whales, dolphins, and fish, and open the door to drilling that could hurt coastal tourism and fishing economies. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents, commercial and recreational fishing interests, and the tourism economy along the Atlantic seaboard, who would be spared the noise impacts of airgun surveys and the risks that follow from offshore drilling development. Marine mammals and fish populations also stand to benefit from a quieter ocean.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal residents, fisheries, and tourism economies

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any person or federal agency from conducting geological or geophysical (seismic) activities in support of oil, gas, or methane hydrate exploration and development in the Atlantic planning areas, amending the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to do so [S3].

The activities covered are those described in the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management's final programmatic environmental impact statement for Atlantic seismic surveys completed in February 2014, so the ban targets the full set of federally authorized survey methods [S3] [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas exploration companies and seismic survey contractors would lose access to Atlantic exploration; energy companies would lose a first step toward future Atlantic drilling, and the federal government forgoes potential leasing revenue.

drawbacks.text: Blocking seismic surveys forecloses the first step in assessing and potentially developing Atlantic offshore energy resources, which supporters of drilling argue could add domestic energy supply and federal leasing revenue — a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge [S2].

The ban is permanent and absolute ('notwithstanding any other provision of law') for the covered areas, with no periodic review or exception process, which critics would call an inflexible way to manage offshore resources [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades uncertain future energy development and federal leasing revenue for protection of Atlantic marine life and coastal economies from loud seismic surveys and the risk of eventual drilling. The cost falls on a concentrated industry; the benefit is spread across coastal communities and the public, though whether undeveloped offshore resources would have been worth more is a genuine judgment call.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Natural Resources Committee, then passed to a subcommittee on August 4, 2016, and sat there until the two-year Congress ended with no hearing, no vote, and no further action.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Beyer introduced the bill on July 14, 2016, with six original cosponsors [S1] [S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources [S5].
On August 4, 2016, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, which controlled its fate; no further action followed before the 114th Congress ended January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas exploration interests are better off: no survey ban was enacted, leaving Atlantic seismic testing and future drilling pathways unimpeded by this bill. Coastal communities did not get the protections the bill offered.

for.name: Rep. Don Beyer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban Atlantic seismic airgun surveys for oil and gas exploration

for.name: Original cosponsors including Reps. LoBiondo, Connolly, Price (NC), Langevin, Van Hollen, and Scott (VA)
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction; the bill drew 16 cosponsors total, 14 Democrats and 2 Republicans

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 14, 2016 and never held a markup or advanced the bill; it was passed to a subcommittee where it died

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 14 of 16 cosponsors were Democrats — but two of 246 House Republicans also cosponsored, and the bill never reached a vote where partisan alignment could be measured [S4].

industries.industry: Oil and gas exploration and seismic survey companies
industries.note: The bill would bar seismic surveys that are the entry step to Atlantic drilling, costing these companies an exploration frontier. The surveys blast loud sound pulses through waters used by whales, dolphins, and fish, and can precede drilling that coastal fishing and tourism economies worry about.

industries.industry: Atlantic commercial and recreational fishing and coastal tourism
industries.note: A quieter ocean without airgun surveys protects marine species that fisheries depend on, and the bill stops a first step toward offshore drilling that coastal economies have opposed. Ordinary coastal workers and consumers benefit alongside these industries.
